content.content:
1	# Warehouse Robot Fleet Simulator
2	
3	A small, deterministic Python simulator for experimenting with warehouse maps,
4	robot fleets, task assignment, collision avoidance, route execution, replay, and
5	efficiency metrics. It runs locally and has no runtime dependencies outside the
6	Python standard library.
7	
8	## Quick start
9	
10	```bash
11	python3 -m warehouse_fleet demo --steps 12
12	```
13	
14	The command builds a sample grid, assigns pickup-and-delivery tasks to available
15	robots, advances the fleet one tick at a time, and prints a JSON replay summary.
16	
17	Run the tests with:
18	
19	```bash
20	python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
21	```
22	
23	The public Python API exposes `GridMap`, `Robot`, `Task`, `FleetSimulator`, and
24	`shortest_path` for programmatic scenarios.
25	
26	## Taking over in-flight work
27	
28	A fleet does not have to start idle: `FleetSimulator` accepts robots and tasks
29	that are already mid-work, so a scenario can be handed over exactly where an
30	earlier run (or another tool) left off. Construction only validates and adopts
31	the state — it never advances the clock, moves a robot, or rewrites mileage or
32	completion flags:
33	
34	```python
35	from warehouse_fleet import FleetSimulator, GridMap, Robot, Task
36	
37	grid = GridMap(width=4, height=2, obstacles=frozenset({(1, 0)}))
38	
39	# R-1 collected T-1's goods earlier and is mid-delivery, detouring around
40	# the obstacle at (1, 0) towards the dropoff at (3, 0).
41	carrier = Robot(
42	    "R-1",
43	    position=(0, 0),
44	    route=[(0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 0)],
45	    task_id="T-1",
46	    distance_travelled=5,
47	)
48	in_flight = Task("T-1", pickup=(0, 0), dropoff=(3, 0),
49	                 assigned_robot="R-1", picked_up=True)
50	# A finished delivery kept as history; R-9 need not be in this fleet.
51	history = Task("T-0", pickup=(2, 0), dropoff=(3, 1),
52	               assigned_robot="R-9", picked_up=True, completed=True)
53	
54	simulator = FleetSimulator(grid, [carrier], [in_flight, history])
55	```
56	
57	Right after construction the clock is zero, the replay is empty, no robot has
58	moved, and the mileage and task flags passed in stand unchanged:
59	
60	```python
61	simulator.status()
62	# {'tick': 0, 'width': 4, 'height': 2, 'obstacles': [[1, 0]],
63	#  'paused_tasks': [], 'traffic_waits': []}
64	simulator.metrics()
65	# {'ticks': 0, 'tasks_total': 2, 'tasks_completed': 1, ...}  # T-0 already counts
66	```
67	
68	Because T-1 is already picked up, its remaining route leads only to the
69	dropoff: the robot walks those cells one per tick and never returns to the
70	pickup cell. Each `step()` advances the clock by one, and each cell a robot
71	actually enters adds one to its mileage:
72	
73	```python
74	for _ in range(5):
75	    simulator.step()
76	
77	simulator.robots["R-1"].position            # (3, 0)
78	simulator.robots["R-1"].task_id             # None — released on delivery
79	simulator.robots["R-1"].distance_travelled  # 10 = 5 carried over + 5 driven
80	simulator.tasks["T-1"].completed            # True
81	simulator.tasks["T-1"].assigned_robot       # 'R-1' — kept as the finisher
82	simulator.metrics()["tasks_completed"]      # 2 — history plus the new delivery
83	```
84	
85	Once the route is exhausted on the dropoff cell the task completes, the robot
86	is unbound from it (and becomes available for new assignments), and the task
87	keeps the id of the robot that finished it.
88	
89	### Unique identifiers
90	
91	Each robot id may appear at most once in the robot list and each task id at
92	most once in the task list of a construction request; the two lists have
93	independent namespaces, so a robot and a task may share one string. The
94	identifier alone decides — nothing about the rest of two records can make a
95	clash legal:
96	
97	- two robots with the same id but different positions (or the same position),
98	  different idle state, preset routes or current tasks;
99	- two tasks with the same id but different pickup/dropoff points, owners or
100	  completion state — including one already finished beside one still waiting;
101	- the very same object, or an identical copy, passed in twice.
102	
103	In every such case the whole request is rejected with `ValueError` — the
104	message says whether the clash is among the robots or the tasks and quotes the
105	duplicated id. No record is kept in preference to another, nothing is merged,
106	and nothing is renamed. The check is read-only and runs before any other
107	normalization commits, so even a duplicate at the end of either list leaves
108	every earlier `Robot` and `Task` exactly as supplied — positions, list-shaped
109	routes and points, bindings, mileage and completion flags all keep their
110	original containers and values.
111	
112	A task's `assigned_robot` is only a reference, never a second robot entry:
113	several completed tasks may keep the same historical robot, which may even be
114	absent from the fleet. Conversely, tasks with distinct ids but identical
115	pickup/dropoff points are separate tasks — both are kept, assigned and counted
116	independently.
117	
118	### Ownership of in-flight tasks
119	
120	Work still in progress must be bound consistently in both directions: a robot
121	that names a current task must name one that exists, is unfinished, and is
122	assigned back to that same robot, and an unfinished task that names an owner
123	must name an existing robot whose current task it is. A task whose goods are
124	already collected may never lack its carrier — `picked_up=True` with
125	`assigned_robot=None` is rejected. One robot can therefore never be claimed by
126	two unfinished tasks.
127	
128	A completed task is a fixed historical record, not work in progress. It must
129	carry both the picked-up mark and the id of the robot that finished it (a
130	`None` owner means the record is missing, not an anonymous completion), but
131	that robot is history only: it need not be in the fleet, may be idle, or may
132	already work another task. Historical records never occupy a robot and never
133	re-enter task assignment — but they do count towards `metrics()` completion,
134	as the `tasks_completed: 1` above shows. Unassigned, not-yet-collected tasks
135	simply wait and are not an ownership error.
136	
137	Inconsistent input is rejected as a whole: binding a robot to a completed
138	task, pointing a robot at a task owned by someone else, or any other
139	contradiction above raises `ValueError` naming the robot or task involved.
140	Nothing is rebound, unassigned, or dropped, and the caller's `Robot` and
141	`Task` objects are left exactly as passed in — positions, routes and bindings
142	included.
143	
144	```python
145	stray = Robot("R-2", position=(1, 1), task_id="T-0")  # T-0 is completed
146	FleetSimulator(grid, [carrier, stray], [in_flight, history])
147	# ValueError: robot 'R-2' executes task 'T-0' that is already completed
148	```
149	
150	### Task coordinates
151	
152	Every task's `pickup` and `dropoff` must be a list or tuple holding exactly
153	two plain integers, and the two spellings may be mixed freely within one task
154	or batch. Booleans are not integers, and a float is rejected even when it
155	equals an integer value (`1.0` is not `1`); strings, `None`, scalars, missing
156	or extra components, and any other non-coordinate input raise `ValueError`
157	naming the task and whether its pickup or dropoff is at fault. Nothing is
158	rounded, padded, or type-converted. Accepted points are normalized to fresh
159	integer tuples — `[1, 0]` and `(1, 0)` name the same cell, so container type
160	can never make a robot miss a pickup or fail a delivery — and the copy means
161	mutating a coordinate list you passed in after construction never changes the
162	fleet. The rule applies to tasks in every state (waiting, assigned, loaded,
163	completed) and, like positions, commits only once the whole batch passes, so a
164	later bad point, ownership conflict, or route error leaves every earlier
165	`Robot` and `Task` object — containers, routes, bindings, mileage and flags —
166	exactly as passed in. Coordinate validity is separate from reachability: a
167	well-formed task no robot can currently reach simply keeps waiting, and a
168	loaded task whose pickup cell has since been closed keeps the goods and its
169	owner.
170	
171	### Remaining routes for in-flight tasks
172	
173	A robot's remaining route omits its current cell: the first waypoint must be
174	an up/down/left/right neighbour of the current position, and every later
175	waypoint exactly one orthogonal step from the previous one. Every waypoint
176	must lie inside the map and outside the initial obstacles. The route need not
177	be shortest — legal detours and revisiting old cells are fine — and it is
178	judged purely as a walk: crossing another robot's cell is traffic to be
179	settled while stepping, not an error.
180	
181	The two entry points differ in how much they promise. Direct construction
182	checks that the route is a legal walk on the given map; it does not fill in
183	missing pickup or dropoff legs for you, so accepting a route is not a
184	guarantee that the bound task will complete along it — the example above
185	works because its route was chosen to actually reach the dropoff.
186	`FleetSimulator.load_checkpoint` is stricter: every in-flight task must be
187	completable along its robot's remaining route (a non-empty route ends at the
188	dropoff, and a robot that has not collected yet must still pass the pickup).
189	Fleets built through either entry point then behave identically: map edits,
190	yielding and save/restore apply to them exactly as described below.
191	
192	## Closing and reopening cells at runtime
193	
194	Between ticks you may change the map with one batch call. The edit takes effect
195	immediately but neither advances the clock, moves a robot, nor adds mileage:
196	
197	```python
198	simulator.modify_obstacles(added=[(3, 2), (3, 3)], removed=[(5, 4)])
199	```
200	
201	Coordinates must be plain two-integer pairs (booleans are not integers). The
202	whole request is validated up front and rejected with `ValueError` if a
203	coordinate is out of bounds or malformed, a cell is both added and removed, or
204	a newly added obstacle covers a robot's current cell; on rejection the map,
205	routes, tasks, statistics and history are all left untouched. Duplicate
206	coordinates inside one batch are processed once; adding an already blocked
207	cell or removing a traversable cell is a no-op, and a batch with no actual
208	effect produces no change record.
209	
210	After an accepted edit every assigned, unfinished task keeps its robot. A robot
211	that has not picked up replans a shortest feasible route from its current cell
212	through the pickup point to the dropoff (a robot already at the pickup point
213	collects first at the next step); a robot carrying goods routes straight to the
214	dropoff and never returns to a subsequently closed pickup cell. If any required
215	cell is unreachable, the robot's remaining route is cleared and the task is
216	*paused* — it is neither driven along a stale route, released, nor completed.
217	Unassigned tasks whose points are unreachable simply keep waiting and never
218	block other tasks. The next `step()` after cells reopen automatically resumes
219	paused driving and assigns waiting tasks; collision avoidance still applies and
220	robots never enter a new obstacle.
221	
222	A robot without a bound task that is still driving a preset route is treated
223	differently: closing a cell on its remaining route neither clears nor replans
224	that route. The robot keeps every unconsumed waypoint, drives the cells still
225	open before the closure, and then simply waits in front of the closed cell —
226	waiting consumes no waypoint and adds no mileage. When the cell reopens it
227	continues the same route in the same order; it never picks a shortcut and
228	never skips the blocked waypoint. Such a waiting state saves and restores
229	through checkpoints (see below).
230	
231	Queries and history:
232	
233	```python
234	simulator.status()              # current obstacles + paused task ids + traffic waits
235	simulator.map_change_history()  # effective tick, adds/removes, order
236	```
237	
238	`status()` reports tasks paused because the map made their route infeasible,
239	which is distinct from a robot briefly waiting for another robot to clear the
240	way. Every *actual* change is stored both in the dedicated history and in the
241	replay as a `map_change` event carrying the tick it took effect at, its global
242	sequence number (consecutive edits at the same tick keep their order), and the
243	added/removed cells; ordinary tick frames keep their original positions and
244	completion data and are never rewritten by later maps. Identical initial state
245	with an identical sequence of steps and edits always produces identical
246	routes, replay and statistics.
247	
248	## Automatic yielding in traffic
249	
250	When a robot's next waypoint is occupied by another robot, `step()` no longer
251	just waits: a parked blocker — one with no bound task *and* no remaining
252	route — is asked to step onto a free neighbouring cell that lies on no
253	robot's planned route, and a busy robot whose blocker cannot drive on may
254	sidestep onto a free adjacent cell itself and replan its (still shortest)
255	route from there. A taskless robot that still carries a remaining route is
256	not parked: it drives that route cell by cell just like a task-bound robot,
257	is never pushed off it for another robot, and when its own next cell is
258	occupied it simply stays put with its unconsumed waypoints — an open side
259	cell changes nothing. Only once that route is finished does it become a
260	parked robot that yields by the side-cell rule. Every robot still moves at
261	most one orthogonal cell per tick (or waits), robots never share a cell at
262	the end of a tick, never swap places within one tick, and never enter an
263	obstacle.
264	
265	A sidestep that cannot make progress is not taken. If the replanned route
266	steps straight back through the cell the robot is vacating, still runs past
267	the same blocker's cell, and the blocker cannot use the opening to get out of
268	the way (for example an idle robot parked at the end of a one-wide corridor
269	with no neighbouring cell to yield onto), the robot waits instead of
270	retreating and shuttling back to the identical blockage on the next tick.
271	More empty cells behind the waiting robot do not change this. A sidestep that
272	genuinely routes around the blocker, or a retreat the blocker immediately
273	drives into to clear the way, is still driven.
274	
275	Yielding moves count as mileage; waiting does not. The task keeps its
276	original robot and the pickup rules are unchanged — goods are collected
277	before delivery, a loaded robot never returns to the pickup cell, and nothing
278	completes early because of a detour. Robots paused by map unreachability stay
279	put and never take part in yielding. An idle robot that yields is not hired
280	by doing so: it stays on its side cell once the way is clear and can still
281	pick up tasks later. If no safe side cell exists, both robots simply wait —
282	time advances, cargo and tasks are kept, and nothing collides or completes.
283	
284	Traffic waits are reported separately from map pauses:
285	
286	```python
287	simulator.status()["traffic_waits"]
288	# [{"robot_id": "R-01", "blocked_by": ["R-02"], "ticks": 3}, ...]
289	```
290	
291	A robot's counter only grows while it stops for traffic and another robot
292	still blocks its next waypoint once the tick's moves have settled; any move or
293	the blockage clearing resets it to zero. A blocker that advances later in the
294	same tick is not a blockage at tick end, so that tick adds nothing. If the
295	wait never breaks but the robot holding the next cell merely changes, the
296	count continues with the new blocker; once the wait was actually interrupted,
297	a later blockage starts again at one. The
298	same report appears in `metrics()` (and therefore in the command-line
299	output), and it is saved into and restored from checkpoints — older
300	checkpoint files without it load with every counter at zero.
301	
302	
303	## Saving and resuming progress
304	
305	State can be saved after any tick and resumed later in a new process. From
306	Python, `FleetSimulator.save_checkpoint(path)` writes the state without
307	advancing the tick or mutating the simulator, and the class method
308	`FleetSimulator.load_checkpoint(path)` returns an independent simulator:
309	loading the same file twice gives two instances whose subsequent runs never
310	interfere with each other.
311	
312	```python
313	simulator.save_checkpoint("fleet.json")
314	restored = FleetSimulator.load_checkpoint("fleet.json")
315	```
316	
317	Writes are atomic: an existing checkpoint file always contains either the
318	complete old contents or the complete new contents, and a failed save to a new
319	path leaves no partial file behind. Filesystem and permission failures raise
320	`OSError`; malformed or inconsistent checkpoint content raises `ValueError`
321	with the reason.
322	
323	The command line can save at the end of a run and continue from a checkpoint:
324	
325	```bash
326	python3 -m warehouse_fleet demo --steps 6 --checkpoint fleet.json
327	python3 -m warehouse_fleet resume fleet.json --steps 20
328	```
329	
330	`resume FILE --steps N` runs at most `N` more ticks and stops early once every
331	task is complete. When the checkpoint is already complete, or `N` is `0`, the
332	current state is printed without advancing. Add `--checkpoint OUT` to save the
333	updated state; without it the source file is left untouched, and naming the
334	same file updates it in place. Both commands print the same JSON snapshot and
335	report any load/save error on standard error with a non-zero exit code.
336	
337	### Checkpoint file format (version 2)
338	
339	Checkpoints are UTF-8 encoded JSON. The top-level object contains:
340	
341	- `version` — integer format version, currently `2`. Version `1` files remain
342	  loadable and are interpreted as having no map-modification history.
343	- `grid` — `{"width", "height", "obstacles"}`, the map *currently in effect*,
344	  where obstacles is a list of `[x, y]` cells.
345	- `base_grid` — same shape as `grid`; the map before any runtime edit. Replaying
346	  the change history against it must reproduce `grid`.
347	- `tick` — number of ticks already executed.
348	- `robots` — list of `{"robot_id", "position", "route", "task_id",
349	  "distance_travelled"}`; `position` is `[x, y]` and `route` is the remaining
350	  waypoints after the current position (empty for a paused robot).
351	- `tasks` — list of `{"task_id", "pickup", "dropoff", "assigned_robot",
352	  "picked_up", "completed"}`. Completed tasks keep their historical
353	  `assigned_robot`; unassigned tasks use `null`.
354	- `paused_tasks` — ids of tasks whose assigned robot currently cannot reach a
355	  required point on the saved map.
356	- `traffic_waits` — optional list of `{"robot_id", "blocked_by", "ticks"}`
357	  entries: robots currently held up by other robots, who blocks them, and for
358	  how many consecutive ticks. Older files without this field load with every
359	  counter at zero.
360	- `map_changes` — every actual edit in order, each
361	  `{"tick", "sequence", "added", "removed"}`; `sequence` runs from 1 and
362	  consecutive edits at the same `tick` preserve their order.
363	- `replay` — ordered events. Tick frames are `{"type": "tick", "tick", "moved",
364	  "robots", "completed"}`, numbered consecutively from `1` through `tick`.
365	  Map-change frames are interspersed at their effective tick and have the shape
366	  `{"type": "map_change", "tick", "sequence", "added", "removed"}`. In any
367	  non-zero-tick file the last tick frame's robot positions must equal the
368	  current robot positions; historical frames are never overwritten by later
369	  maps.
370	
371	Loading validates the entire document: corrupted JSON, missing or wrongly
372	typed fields, unsupported versions, duplicate robot or task ids, overlapping
373	or out-of-bounds/blocked robot positions, routes that leave the map, cross
374	obstacles unexplained by the change history, make non-adjacent moves, or
375	cannot complete the robot's bound task, task/robot ownership mismatches, a
376	broken replay history, out-of-bounds or add/remove-conflicting change
377	records,
378	a change history that does not reproduce the saved grid, and an inconsistent
379	paused-task state are all rejected. So is a replay whose *history* could never
380	have happened, even when its final frame matches the saved robots: a robot out
381	of bounds or on an obstacle that existed at that tick, two robots sharing a
382	cell at a tick boundary, a jump of more than one orthogonal cell or a two-robot
383	cell swap between neighboring tick frames, and a `moved` list that names an
384	unknown/duplicated robot or does not exactly match the robots that changed
385	position (following another robot into the cell it just vacated is legal, and
386	the list need not be sorted). Map edits are judged against contemporary
387	positions: a cell a robot once passed through may be closed later without
388	invalidating the replay, a robot may not appear in a cell before it opens, and
389	an edit may not add an obstacle onto a cell occupied when that tick ended —
390	not even if another edit of the same tick removes it again. The first tick
391	frame has no recorded predecessor, so its cells, overlaps and `moved` ids are
392	still checked but the first moves are not second-guessed; zero-tick files,
393	empty fleets and all-waiting frames remain valid. Beyond physical
394	plausibility, each assigned, unfinished, non-paused task must still be
395	completable along its robot's remaining route: a non-empty route has to end at
396	the dropoff, and a robot that has not collected yet — unless it is already
397	standing on the pickup cell — must still pass through the pickup (visiting the
398	dropoff early and leaving again is fine; detours need not match a replanned
399	shortest path). An empty route is accepted only for a loaded robot already at
400	the dropoff, or when position, pickup and dropoff all coincide; map-paused
401	tasks keep their empty-route exemption. Version 1 documents contain
402	tick frames without a `type` field and none of the edit-related keys; they
403	load as if no map edit had ever happened.
404	
405	The one blocked-waypoint route a version 2 checkpoint accepts belongs to a
406	robot with no bound task that is waiting out a dynamic closure: the blocked
407	waypoint must have been traversable on the initial map, a valid map change
408	must have closed it, and it must still be closed in the saved grid — exactly
409	the state normal running produces when a preset route reaches a cell that was
410	later shut. Saving and loading preserve the position, the remaining waypoint
411	order, the mileage and the change history without advancing time or moving
412	the robot; on resume the robot finishes the still-open waypoints, waits
413	without consuming a waypoint or gaining mileage, and continues the original
414	route from the next cell once the way reopens, never detouring or skipping.
415	The exemption is narrow: creating a fleet directly still rejects a route
416	through an initial obstacle, a blocked waypoint that the change history
417	cannot explain is rejected, task-bound robots keep their reroute/pause rules,
418	and version 1 files keep the old requirement. A robot standing on an
419	obstacle, an out-of-map or non-integer waypoint, and a jump between waypoints
420	are rejected regardless.
421	
422

# Warehouse Robot Fleet Simulator

A small, deterministic Python simulator for experimenting with warehouse maps,
robot fleets, task assignment, collision avoidance, route execution, replay, and
efficiency metrics. It runs locally and has no runtime dependencies outside the
Python standard library.

## Quick start

```bash
python3 -m warehouse_fleet demo --steps 12
```

The command builds a sample grid, assigns pickup-and-delivery tasks to available
robots, advances the fleet one tick at a time, and prints a JSON replay summary.

Run the tests with:

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

The public Python API exposes `GridMap`, `Robot`, `Task`, `FleetSimulator`, and
`shortest_path` for programmatic scenarios.

## Taking over in-flight work

A fleet does not have to start idle: `FleetSimulator` accepts robots and tasks
that are already mid-work, so a scenario can be handed over exactly where an
earlier run (or another tool) left off. Construction only validates and adopts
the state — it never advances the clock, moves a robot, or rewrites mileage or
completion flags:

```python
from warehouse_fleet import FleetSimulator, GridMap, Robot, Task

grid = GridMap(width=4, height=2, obstacles=frozenset({(1, 0)}))

# R-1 collected T-1's goods earlier and is mid-delivery, detouring around
# the obstacle at (1, 0) towards the dropoff at (3, 0).
carrier = Robot(
    "R-1",
    position=(0, 0),
    route=[(0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 0)],
    task_id="T-1",
    distance_travelled=5,
)
in_flight = Task("T-1", pickup=(0, 0), dropoff=(3, 0),
                 assigned_robot="R-1", picked_up=True)
# A finished delivery kept as history; R-9 need not be in this fleet.
history = Task("T-0", pickup=(2, 0), dropoff=(3, 1),
               assigned_robot="R-9", picked_up=True, completed=True)

simulator = FleetSimulator(grid, [carrier], [in_flight, history])
```

Right after construction the clock is zero, the replay is empty, no robot has
moved, and the mileage and task flags passed in stand unchanged:

```python
simulator.status()
# {'tick': 0, 'width': 4, 'height': 2, 'obstacles': [[1, 0]],
#  'paused_tasks': [], 'traffic_waits': []}
simulator.metrics()
# {'ticks': 0, 'tasks_total': 2, 'tasks_completed': 1, ...}  # T-0 already counts
```

Because T-1 is already picked up, its remaining route leads only to the
dropoff: the robot walks those cells one per tick and never returns to the
pickup cell. Each `step()` advances the clock by one, and each cell a robot
actually enters adds one to its mileage:

```python
for _ in range(5):
    simulator.step()

simulator.robots["R-1"].position            # (3, 0)
simulator.robots["R-1"].task_id             # None — released on delivery
simulator.robots["R-1"].distance_travelled  # 10 = 5 carried over + 5 driven
simulator.tasks["T-1"].completed            # True
simulator.tasks["T-1"].assigned_robot       # 'R-1' — kept as the finisher
simulator.metrics()["tasks_completed"]      # 2 — history plus the new delivery
```

Once the route is exhausted on the dropoff cell the task completes, the robot
is unbound from it (and becomes available for new assignments), and the task
keeps the id of the robot that finished it.

Each robot id may appear at most once in the robot list and each task id at
most once in the task list of a construction request; the two lists have
independent namespaces, so a robot and a task may share one string. The
identifier alone decides — nothing about the rest of two records can make a
clash legal:

- two robots with the same id but different positions (or the same position),
  different idle state, preset routes or current tasks;
- two tasks with the same id but different pickup/dropoff points, owners or
  completion state — including one already finished beside one still waiting;
- the very same object, or an identical copy, passed in twice.

robots never enter a new obstacle.

A robot without a bound task that is still driving a preset route is treated
differently: closing a cell on its remaining route neither clears nor replans
that route. The robot keeps every unconsumed waypoint, drives the cells still
open before the closure, and then simply waits in front of the closed cell —
waiting consumes no waypoint and adds no mileage. When the cell reopens it
continues the same route in the same order; it never picks a shortcut and
never skips the blocked waypoint. Such a waiting state saves and restores
through checkpoints (see below).

Queries and history:

```python
simulator.status()              # current obstacles + paused task ids + traffic waits
simulator.map_change_history()  # effective tick, adds/removes, order
```

`status()` reports tasks paused because the map made their route infeasible,
which is distinct from a robot briefly waiting for another robot to clear the
way. Every *actual* change is stored both in the dedicated history and in the
replay as a `map_change` event carrying the tick it took effect at, its global
sequence number (consecutive edits at the same tick keep their order), and the
added/removed cells; ordinary tick frames keep their original positions and
completion data and are never rewritten by later maps. Identical initial state
with an identical sequence of steps and edits always produces identical
routes, replay and statistics.

## Automatic yielding in traffic

When a robot's next waypoint is occupied by another robot, `step()` no longer
just waits: a parked blocker — one with no bound task *and* no remaining
route — is asked to step onto a free neighbouring cell that lies on no
robot's planned route, and a busy robot whose blocker cannot drive on may
sidestep onto a free adjacent cell itself and replan its (still shortest)
route from there. A taskless robot that still carries a remaining route is
not parked: it drives that route cell by cell just like a task-bound robot,
is never pushed off it for another robot, and when its own next cell is
occupied it simply stays put with its unconsumed waypoints — an open side
cell changes nothing. Only once that route is finished does it become a
parked robot that yields by the side-cell rule. Every robot still moves at
most one orthogonal cell per tick (or waits), robots never share a cell at
the end of a tick, never swap places within one tick, and never enter an
obstacle.

A sidestep that cannot make progress is not taken. If the replanned route
steps straight back through the cell the robot is vacating, still runs past
the same blocker's cell, and the blocker cannot use the opening to get out of
the way (for example an idle robot parked at the end of a one-wide corridor
with no neighbouring cell to yield onto), the robot waits instead of
retreating and shuttling back to the identical blockage on the next tick.
More empty cells behind the waiting robot do not change this. A sidestep that
genuinely routes around the blocker, or a retreat the blocker immediately
drives into to clear the way, is still driven.

Yielding moves count as mileage; waiting does not. The task keeps its
original robot and the pickup rules are unchanged — goods are collected
before delivery, a loaded robot never returns to the pickup cell, and nothing
completes early because of a detour. Robots paused by map unreachability stay
put and never take part in yielding. An idle robot that yields is not hired
by doing so: it stays on its side cell once the way is clear and can still
pick up tasks later. If no safe side cell exists, both robots simply wait —
time advances, cargo and tasks are kept, and nothing collides or completes.

Traffic waits are reported separately from map pauses:

```python
simulator.status()["traffic_waits"]
# [{"robot_id": "R-01", "blocked_by": ["R-02"], "ticks": 3}, ...]
```

A robot's counter only grows while it stops for traffic and another robot
still blocks its next waypoint once the tick's moves have settled; any move or
the blockage clearing resets it to zero. A blocker that advances later in the
same tick is not a blockage at tick end, so that tick adds nothing. If the
wait never breaks but the robot holding the next cell merely changes, the
count continues with the new blocker; once the wait was actually interrupted,
a later blockage starts again at one. The
same report appears in `metrics()` (and therefore in the command-line
output), and it is saved into and restored from checkpoints — older
checkpoint files without it load with every counter at zero.


## Saving and resuming progress

State can be saved after any tick and resumed later in a new process. From
Python, `FleetSimulator.save_checkpoint(path)` writes the state without
advancing the tick or mutating the simulator, and the class method
`FleetSimulator.load_checkpoint(path)` returns an independent simulator:
loading the same file twice gives two instances whose subsequent runs never
interfere with each other.

```python
simulator.save_checkpoint("fleet.json")
restored = FleetSimulator.load_checkpoint("fleet.json")
```

Writes are atomic: an existing checkpoint file always contains either the
complete old contents or the complete new contents, and a failed save to a new
path leaves no partial file behind. Filesystem and permission failures raise
`OSError`; malformed or inconsistent checkpoint content raises `ValueError`
with the reason.

The command line can save at the end of a run and continue from a checkpoint:

```bash
python3 -m warehouse_fleet demo --steps 6 --checkpoint fleet.json
python3 -m warehouse_fleet resume fleet.json --steps 20
```

`resume FILE --steps N` runs at most `N` more ticks and stops early once every
task is complete. When the checkpoint is already complete, or `N` is `0`, the
current state is printed without advancing. Add `--checkpoint OUT` to save the
updated state; without it the source file is left untouched, and naming the
same file updates it in place. Both commands print the same JSON snapshot and
report any load/save error on standard error with a non-zero exit code.

### Checkpoint file format (version 2)

Checkpoints are UTF-8 encoded JSON. The top-level object contains:

- `version` — integer format version, currently `2`. Version `1` files remain
  loadable and are interpreted as having no map-modification history.
- `grid` — `{"width", "height", "obstacles"}`, the map *currently in effect*,
  where obstacles is a list of `[x, y]` cells.
- `base_grid` — same shape as `grid`; the map before any runtime edit. Replaying
  the change history against it must reproduce `grid`.
- `tick` — number of ticks already executed.
- `robots` — list of `{"robot_id", "position", "route", "task_id",
  "distance_travelled"}`; `position` is `[x, y]` and `route` is the remaining
  waypoints after the current position (empty for a paused robot).
- `tasks` — list of `{"task_id", "pickup", "dropoff", "assigned_robot",
  "picked_up", "completed"}`. Completed tasks keep their historical
  `assigned_robot`; unassigned tasks use `null`.
- `paused_tasks` — ids of tasks whose assigned robot currently cannot reach a
  required point on the saved map.
- `traffic_waits` — optional list of `{"robot_id", "blocked_by", "ticks"}`
  entries: robots currently held up by other robots, who blocks them, and for
  how many consecutive ticks. Older files without this field load with every
  counter at zero.
- `map_changes` — every actual edit in order, each
  `{"tick", "sequence", "added", "removed"}`; `sequence` runs from 1 and
  consecutive edits at the same `tick` preserve their order.
- `replay` — ordered events. Tick frames are `{"type": "tick", "tick", "moved",
  "robots", "completed"}`, numbered consecutively from `1` through `tick`.
  Map-change frames are interspersed at their effective tick and have the shape
  `{"type": "map_change", "tick", "sequence", "added", "removed"}`. In any
  non-zero-tick file the last tick frame's robot positions must equal the
  current robot positions; historical frames are never overwritten by later
  maps.

Loading validates the entire document: corrupted JSON, missing or wrongly
typed fields, unsupported versions, duplicate robot or task ids, overlapping
or out-of-bounds/blocked robot positions, routes that leave the map, cross
obstacles unexplained by the change history, make non-adjacent moves, or
cannot complete the robot's bound task, task/robot ownership mismatches, a
broken replay history, out-of-bounds or add/remove-conflicting change
records,
a change history that does not reproduce the saved grid, and an inconsistent
paused-task state are all rejected. So is a replay whose *history* could never
have happened, even when its final frame matches the saved robots: a robot out
of bounds or on an obstacle that existed at that tick, two robots sharing a
cell at a tick boundary, a jump of more than one orthogonal cell or a two-robot
cell swap between neighboring tick frames, and a `moved` list that names an
unknown/duplicated robot or does not exactly match the robots that changed
position (following another robot into the cell it just vacated is legal, and
the list need not be sorted). Map edits are judged against contemporary
positions: a cell a robot once passed through may be closed later without
invalidating the replay, a robot may not appear in a cell before it opens, and
an edit may not add an obstacle onto a cell occupied when that tick ended —
not even if another edit of the same tick removes it again. The first tick
frame has no recorded predecessor, so its cells, overlaps and `moved` ids are
still checked but the first moves are not second-guessed; zero-tick files,
empty fleets and all-waiting frames remain valid. Beyond physical
plausibility, each assigned, unfinished, non-paused task must still be
completable along its robot's remaining route: a non-empty route has to end at
the dropoff, and a robot that has not collected yet — unless it is already
standing on the pickup cell — must still pass through the pickup (visiting the
dropoff early and leaving again is fine; detours need not match a replanned
shortest path). An empty route is accepted only for a loaded robot already at
the dropoff, or when position, pickup and dropoff all coincide; map-paused
tasks keep their empty-route exemption. Version 1 documents contain
tick frames without a `type` field and none of the edit-related keys; they
load as if no map edit had ever happened.

The one blocked-waypoint route a version 2 checkpoint accepts belongs to a
robot with no bound task that is waiting out a dynamic closure: the blocked
waypoint must have been traversable on the initial map, a valid map change
must have closed it, and it must still be closed in the saved grid — exactly
the state normal running produces when a preset route reaches a cell that was
later shut. Saving and loading preserve the position, the remaining waypoint
order, the mileage and the change history without advancing time or moving
the robot; on resume the robot finishes the still-open waypoints, waits
without consuming a waypoint or gaining mileage, and continues the original
route from the next cell once the way reopens, never detouring or skipping.
The exemption is narrow: creating a fleet directly still rejects a route
through an initial obstacle, a blocked waypoint that the change history
cannot explain is rejected, task-bound robots keep their reroute/pause rules,
and version 1 files keep the old requirement. A robot standing on an
obstacle, an out-of-map or non-integer waypoint, and a jump between waypoints
are rejected regardless.

232	    Map-change events sit between ticks (or after the last tick) and look like
233	    ``{"type": "map_change", "tick": int, "sequence": int,
234	    "added": [[x, y], ...], "removed": [[x, y], ...]}``. When ``tick`` is
235	    non-zero the final tick event's robot positions must match the current
236	    robot positions.
237	``map_changes`` (version 2 only)
238	    List mirroring the replay map-change events in the same order:
239	    ``{"tick": int, "sequence": int, "added": [...], "removed": [...]}``.
240	``base_grid`` (version 2 only)
241	    ``{"width", "height", "obstacles"}`` describing the map before any runtime
242	    edit. Replaying ``map_changes`` against it must reproduce the saved current
243	    ``grid``.
244	``traffic_waits`` (optional)
245	    List of ``{"robot_id": str, "blocked_by": [str, ...], "ticks": int}``
246	    entries recording how many consecutive ticks each robot has been held up
247	    purely by other robots. Absent in older files, which load with every
248	    wait counter at zero. Each entry must agree with the saved layout: the
249	    robot needs a remaining route and ``blocked_by`` must name exactly the
250	    robot occupying its next route cell -- a next cell nobody occupies, a
251	    listed blocker parked elsewhere, or extra names beside the real blocker
252	    all reject the document.
253	
254	Version 1 documents store tick frames without a ``type`` field and have no
255	``map_changes`` or ``base_grid`` key; they load with their grid taken as the
256	baseline, as if no map edit ever happened.
257	
258	The ordinary-tick-frame rules both versions share -- the replay container is
259	a list, every frame is an object, and tick frames are numbered consecutively
260	from 1 with a well-formed payload -- are owned by the single shared
261	:meth:`FleetSimulator._iter_replay_events` scan, so they are maintained in
262	exactly one place. Each version keeps its own handling on top: version 1
263	rejects non-tick frames and fills in the missing ``type`` on a copy, while
264	version 2 dispatches event types and enforces its map-change ordering.
265	
266	Both map definitions are validated by the single shared
267	:meth:`FleetSimulator._load_map_definition` rule -- positive integer
268	dimensions, an obstacle list of integer ``[x, y]`` pairs inside the map --
269	with wording that names the map at fault, so a format or value rule is
270	maintained in exactly one place while each map keeps its own contents. The
271	cross-definition constraints (matching dimensions and a history that replays
272	``base_grid`` onto ``grid``) are checked separately and remain distinct
273	rejection reasons from a malformed definition.
274	
275	Loading performs strict validation: malformed JSON, missing or wrongly typed
276	fields, unsupported versions, duplicate or inconsistent entities, out of
277	bounds/obstructed positions and routes, non-adjacent route steps, ownership
278	mismatches, routes that cannot finish the robot's bound task, traffic waits
279	that contradict the saved robot positions and remaining routes, broken replay
280	or map-change history, a completion history that contradicts the saved task
281	states, and a history that does not reproduce the saved grid all raise
282	:class:`ValueError`.
283	
284	The single route-walk exception recovery allows is a preset-route robot that
285	is waiting out a dynamic closure. In a version 2 file a robot without a bound
286	task may keep waypoints that are blocked on the saved grid when the base map
287	had the cell open and the recorded change history explains its current,
288	still-effective closure (a cell closed and reopened before the save is open
289	again and therefore never covered). Such a robot was produced by normal
290	running -- closing a cell never strips a taskless robot of its remaining
291	route, the robot just waits before the cell -- so recovery restores it as is
292	and it drives on, same cells, same order, once the cell reopens. The
293	exemption cannot reach anything else: direct fleet construction has no
294	history and rejects routes through initial obstacles, a blocked waypoint the
295	history cannot account for (including every blocked waypoint in a version 1
296	document) is still rejected, and robots bound to a task never qualify --
297	their routes are replanned or their tasks paused at edit time and load under
298	the unchanged task rules. A robot standing on an obstacle and an out-of-map,
299	malformed or non-adjacent waypoint are rejected regardless of task state.
300	
301	A task-bound route is judged against the task's pickup state, not just for
302	walkability. For every assigned, unfinished task that is not paused by map
303	unreachability, a non-empty remaining route must end at the dropoff, and when
304	the goods are not yet collected and the robot is not already standing on the
305	pickup cell, the route must still pass through that pickup cell -- passing the
306	dropoff early changes nothing as long as the route later collects and returns,
307	and avoidance detours need not match a replanned shortest route. An empty
308	route is accepted only when a loaded robot already stands at the dropoff, or
309	when position, pickup and dropoff all coincide; paused tasks keep their
310	empty-route exemption, and unassigned or completed tasks are not checked.
311	
312	The recorded movement history is checked for physical plausibility, not just
313	for a matching final frame. In every tick frame each robot must stand on a
314	cell that is in bounds and traversable on the map of that moment, no two
315	robots may end a tick on the same cell, and from the second frame on a robot
316	may only have waited or stepped one orthogonal cell (two robots cannot swap
317	cells within one tick; following a robot into the cell it just vacated is
318	fine). A frame's ``moved`` list must reference current fleet robots without
319	duplicates and, whenever a previous frame exists, must name exactly the
320	robots whose positions changed, in any order. Version 2 map changes are
321	applied in their recorded order after the tick they are stamped on, so a
322	robot may be recorded in a cell that is closed later, may not appear in a
323	cell before it opens, and no change may add an obstacle onto a cell a tick
324	frame shows occupied -- not even when a later change of the same tick removes
325	it. Filesystem and permission failures propagate as :class:`OSError`.
326	"""

345	def _is_int(value: object) -> bool:
346	    """JSON booleans are ints in Python; checkpoints treat them as wrong."""
347	    return isinstance(value, int) and not isinstance(value, bool)

350	def _coordinate_pair(value: object, description: str, *, strict_list: bool) -> Position:
351	    """Validate *value* as a pair of two plain integers.
352	
353	    Booleans are rejected even though they are Python ints, and wrong lengths
354	    or element types raise :class:`ValueError` instead of leaking unpacking or
355	    hashing errors. This is the one coordinate-shape rule shared by every
356	    caller; the two entry points only differ in the outer container spellings
357	    they accept:
358	
359	    * strict JSON lists only (*strict_list* true, checkpoints, whose document
360	      shape is fixed and must not be relaxed because validation is shared);
361	    * lists or tuples alike (*strict_list* false, the direct Python interface,
362	      where the two spellings may be mixed freely).
363	    """
364	    if strict_list:
365	        # Checkpoints keep their single, fixed message for every shape problem
366	        # -- wrong type, wrong length or a non-integer (including a boolean) --
367	        # because the JSON document shape is fixed and shared validation must
368	        # not change what a malformed checkpoint reports.
369	        if (
370	            not isinstance(value, list)
371	            or len(value) != 2
372	            or not all(_is_int(coord) for coord in value)
373	        ):
374	            raise ValueError(f"{description} must be a [x, y] integer pair")
375	    else:
376	        if isinstance(value, (str, bytes)) or not isinstance(value, (tuple, list)):
377	            raise ValueError(f"{description} must be a [x, y] integer pair")
378	        if len(value) != 2:
379	            raise ValueError(f"{description} must be a [x, y] integer pair")
380	        if not all(_is_int(coord) for coord in value):
381	            raise ValueError(
382	                f"{description} coordinates must be integers, not booleans or other types"
383	            )
384	    return value[0], value[1]

397	def _task_route_waypoints(origin: Position, task: Task) -> list[Position]:
398	    """Required remaining visit points after *origin* for *task*.
399	
400	    The same pickup/delivery rule is used by first-time assignment, rerouting
401	    after map changes (and the recovery/sidestep planning that shares it) and
402	    checkpoint validation, so the requirement lives in exactly one place:
403	
404	    * Goods not yet collected: the route must still reach the pickup and then
405	      the dropoff. Standing exactly on the pickup makes the pickup leg empty --
406	      the leg contributes no waypoint -- but planning never collects or
407	      completes anything by itself.
408	    * Goods already collected: the robot routes straight to the dropoff, even
409	      when the old pickup cell was closed afterwards; it is never sent back.
410	
411	    When *origin*, pickup and dropoff coincide the list is empty, which
412	    describes a feasible zero-step route and must not be confused with an
413	    unreachable one.
414	    """
415	    waypoints: list[Position] = []
416	    if not task.picked_up and origin != task.pickup:
417	        waypoints.append(task.pickup)
418	    last = waypoints[-1] if waypoints else origin
419	    if task.dropoff != last:
420	        waypoints.append(task.dropoff)
421	    return waypoints

424	def _plan_task_route(
425	    grid: GridMap, origin: Position, task: Task
426	) -> list[Position] | None:
427	    """Shortest feasible route through the task's required waypoints.
428	
429	    The returned list holds the cells after *origin* only, concatenating the
430	    deterministic shortest legs between consecutive required points. It is
431	    ``None`` when any required point cannot be reached, and an empty list for a
432	    feasible route with zero steps (origin already at the only destination).
433	    """
434	    route: list[Position] = []
435	    current = origin
436	    for waypoint in _task_route_waypoints(origin, task):
437	        try:
438	            leg = shortest_path(grid, current, waypoint)
439	        except ValueError:
440	            return None
441	        route.extend(leg)
442	        current = waypoint
443	    return route

446	def _validate_route_walk(
447	    grid: GridMap,
448	    origin: Position,
449	    route: Sequence[object],
450	    *,
451	    robot_id: str,
452	    checkpoint: bool,
453	    blocked_cells: frozenset[Position] | None = None,
454	) -> list[Position]:
455	    """Validate one robot's remaining route as a cell-by-cell map walk.
456	
457	    This is the single place that owns the walking rule shared by direct
458	    fleet construction and checkpoint recovery, so the same legality check is
459	    never edited twice. A route holds the cells still ahead of *origin*:
460	
461	    * every waypoint must parse as two plain integers (booleans are rejected),
462	      and lie inside the map -- a cell in *blocked_cells* is the one kind of
463	      currently obstructed waypoint a version 2 checkpoint recovery may carry
464	      (see below), everything else off the traversable map is rejected;
465	    * the first waypoint must be an up/down/left/right neighbour of *origin*,
466	      so a first waypoint equal to the current cell is rejected;
467	    * every later waypoint must be exactly one orthogonal step from the
468	      previous one -- diagonal moves, multi-cell jumps and two identical
469	      consecutive waypoints are all rejected.
470	
471	    Detours and revisits (including *origin*) are legal, and a route crossing
472	    another robot's cell is never a walk error: traffic is settled while
473	    stepping, not here. The walkability rule deliberately says nothing about
474	    the bound task's pickup/dropoff requirements; checkpoint loading keeps
475	    that separate, stricter business check. The result is a fresh mutable list
476	    of tuple cells, so validating never aliases or mutates the caller's
477	    container and a rejected input leaves every earlier object untouched.
478	
479	    *blocked_cells* is honoured only for checkpoint recovery and names the
480	    cells the recorded map-change history explains: cells open on the base map
481	    that an accepted edit has since closed and that are still closed at save
482	    time. A taskless robot's preset route may legitimately end on such a cell
483	    -- the robot keeps its unconsumed waypoints and simply waits before it --
484	    so those waypoints walk as well as the open cells do. The exemption is
485	    deliberately narrow: only checkpoint loading ever supplies the set (direct
486	    construction leaves it ``None``), only a robot without a bound task may
487	    use it (the caller never passes the set for a task route), and the cells
488	    must be inside the map -- an out-of-bounds waypoint is rejected regardless.
489	    A blocked cell in the base map that no edit explains is never part of the
490	    set, so a route crossing an initial or unexplained obstacle stays illegal.
491	
492	    The two entries keep their existing format and wording differences via
493	    *checkpoint*: direct construction (false) accepts a list or tuple route of
494	    list-or-tuple cells and reports ``route waypoint N`` with a dedicated
495	    message for a first waypoint on the current cell and for repeated
496	    consecutive waypoints; checkpoint loading (true) keeps the strict JSON
497	    list-of-lists format (``_as_pair``), says ``route entry`` and folds both
498	    equal-cell cases into its existing non-adjacency message. The checks
499	    performed are identical either way.
500	    """
501	    allowed_blocked = frozenset() if blocked_cells is None else blocked_cells
502	    waypoints: list[Position] = []
503	    previous = origin
504	    for index, cell in enumerate(route):
505	        if checkpoint:
506	            waypoint = _as_pair(
507	                cell, f"robot {robot_id!r} route entry {index}"
508	            )
509	        else:
510	            waypoint = _as_cell(
511	                cell, f"robot {robot_id!r} route waypoint {index}"
512	            )
513	        if not grid.contains(waypoint) or (
514	            waypoint in grid.obstacles and waypoint not in allowed_blocked
515	        ):
516	            if checkpoint:
517	                raise ValueError(
518	                    f"robot {robot_id!r} route entry {list(waypoint)} is "
519	                    "outside the map or inside an obstacle"
520	                )
521	            raise ValueError(
522	                f"robot {robot_id!r} route waypoint {index} "
523	                f"{list(waypoint)} is outside the map or inside an obstacle"
524	            )
525	        if waypoint == previous:
526	            if checkpoint:
527	                # The checkpoint wording treats an equal cell like any other
528	                # non-adjacent step, naming both cells of the offending move.
529	                raise ValueError(
530	                    f"robot {robot_id!r} route moves non-adjacently from "
531	                    f"{list(previous)} to {list(waypoint)}"
532	                )
533	            if index == 0:
534	                raise ValueError(
535	                    f"robot {robot_id!r} route waypoint 0 {list(waypoint)} "
536	                    "is the robot's current cell; the remaining route must "
537	                    "start with the next cell"
538	                )
539	            raise ValueError(
540	                f"robot {robot_id!r} route repeats cell {list(waypoint)} at "
541	                f"consecutive waypoints {index - 1} and {index}"
542	            )
543	        if (
544	            abs(waypoint[0] - previous[0])
545	            + abs(waypoint[1] - previous[1])
546	            != 1
547	        ):
548	            if checkpoint:
549	                raise ValueError(
550	                    f"robot {robot_id!r} route moves non-adjacently from "
551	                    f"{list(previous)} to {list(waypoint)}"
552	                )
553	            if index == 0:
554	                segment = (
555	                    f"from its current position {list(previous)} to route "
556	                    f"waypoint 0 {list(waypoint)}"
557	                )
558	            else:
559	                segment = (
560	                    f"from route waypoint {index - 1} {list(previous)} to "
561	                    f"waypoint {index} {list(waypoint)}"
562	                )
563	            raise ValueError(
564	                f"robot {robot_id!r} route moves non-adjacently {segment}: "
565	                "every step must move one orthogonal cell"
566	            )
567	        waypoints.append(waypoint)
568	        previous = waypoint
569	    return waypoints

572	def _traffic_blockers(
573	    robots: Mapping[str, Robot],
574	    paused_robots: frozenset[str] = frozenset(),
575	) -> dict[str, str]:
576	    """The robot actually holding each waitable robot's next route cell.
577	
578	    This is the single occupancy fact behind every traffic-wait judgement --
579	    tick settlement, obstacle-edit reconciliation and checkpoint validation
580	    all ask it here, so the rule is never re-derived (and never edited) in
581	    several places:
582	
583	    * a robot with no remaining route cannot be held up by traffic;
584	    * a robot paused by map unreachability cannot either -- *paused_robots*
585	      names the robots whose tasks are paused (checkpoint loading need not
586	      pass it: a paused robot's saved route is empty there, so the route
587	      check already excludes it);
588	    * otherwise the blocker is whichever robot occupies ``route[0]`` in the
589	      given layout, never the robot itself (a validated route never starts on
590	      the robot's own cell).
591	
592	    The map itself is deliberately not consulted: a next cell sealed by an
593	    obstacle alone produces no blocker -- waiting on a closure is not
594	    traffic -- and the callers own every other consequence. One cell holds at
595	    most one robot, so each waitable robot maps to at most one blocker.
596	    """
597	    occupied = {robot.position: robot.robot_id for robot in robots.values()}
598	    blockers: dict[str, str] = {}
599	    for robot_id, robot in robots.items():
600	        if robot_id in paused_robots or not robot.route:
601	            continue
602	        occupant_id = occupied.get(robot.route[0])
603	        if occupant_id is not None and occupant_id != robot_id:
604	            blockers[robot_id] = occupant_id
605	    return blockers

608	class FleetSimulator:
609	    def __init__(
610	        self,
611	        grid: GridMap,
612	        robots: list[Robot],
613	        tasks: list[Task],
614	        *,
615	        _routes_prevalidated: bool = False,
616	    ) -> None:
617	        self.grid = grid
618	        # The map as built before any runtime edit; map-change history is
619	        # replayed against this baseline.
620	        self.base_grid = grid
621	        # Identity uniqueness is the first batch check: the same robot id may
622	        # name at most one robot in the request and the same task id at most
623	        # one task. It is read-only and rejects the whole batch before any
624	        # normalization can commit, so a clash leaves every caller object
625	        # exactly as supplied. See :meth:`_require_unique_ids`.
626	        self._require_unique_ids(robots, tasks)
627	        # Starting positions share the route coordinates' strict rule: only a
628	        # list or tuple of two plain integers is accepted (booleans, floats and
629	        # strings never act as coordinates), and every accepted position is
630	        # normalized to a fresh integer tuple before any state is committed.
631	        # Task pickup/dropoff points follow the very same rule. This mirrors
632	        # :meth:`_normalize_initial_routes`: all robots and tasks stay exactly
633	        # as the caller passed them until the whole batch -- positions, task
634	        # points, overlaps, ownership and routes -- has passed.
635	        normalized_positions = self._normalize_start_positions(grid, robots)
636	        normalized_task_points = self._normalize_task_coordinates(tasks)
637	        self.robots = {robot.robot_id: robot for robot in robots}
638	        self.tasks = {task.task_id: task for task in tasks}
639	        self.tick = 0
640	        self.replay: list[dict[str, object]] = []
641	        self.map_changes: list[dict[str, object]] = []
642	        self._map_sequence = 0
643	        self.paused_tasks: set[str] = set()
644	        # Consecutive per-robot waits caused purely by other robots:
645	        # robot_id -> (blocking robot id, consecutive ticks). The one-blocker
646	        # fact and the wait lifecycle live with :func:`_traffic_blockers` and
647	        # :meth:`_settle_traffic_waits`; the ``blocked_by`` list shape exists
648	        # only at the report/checkpoint boundary.
649	        self._traffic_waits: dict[str, tuple[str, int]] = {}
650	        self._validate_task_ownership(robots, tasks)
651	        if _routes_prevalidated:
652	            # Checkpoint recovery has already run the shared
653	            # :func:`_validate_route_walk` itself -- including its one narrow
654	            # checkpoint exemption for a taskless preset route waiting before
655	            # a history-explained closed cell -- so its already-normalized
656	            # routes must not be re-checked here against the saved grid, where
657	            # those legitimate waypoints look obstructed. Its robots are built
658	            # fresh during loading with validated integer-tuple positions too,
659	            # so nothing needs committing here. Every other constructor check
660	            # above still ran.
661	            return
662	        # Accepted positions, routes and task points share one internal shape
663	        # regardless of how the caller spelled them: an integer tuple for the
664	        # position and each pickup/dropoff, and a mutable list of tuple cells
665	        # for the route. The normalized copies are committed together only
666	        # after every robot and task passed validation, so a rejection -- even
667	        # one buried in a later robot's route or task point -- never touches
668	        # the caller's objects: a fleet whose routes fail is rejected with
669	        # every robot still holding the original position object and route and
670	        # every task still holding its original pickup/dropoff containers. See
671	        # :meth:`_normalize_initial_routes`,
672	        # :meth:`_normalize_start_positions` and
673	        # :meth:`_normalize_task_coordinates`.
674	        normalized_routes = self._normalize_initial_routes(
675	            grid, robots, normalized_positions
676	        )
677	        for robot, position, route in zip(robots, normalized_positions, normalized_routes):
678	            robot.position = position
679	            robot.route = route
680	        for task, (pickup, dropoff) in zip(tasks, normalized_task_points):
681	            task.pickup = pickup
682	            task.dropoff = dropoff
683	
684	    @staticmethod
685	    def _require_unique_ids(
686	        robots: Sequence[Robot], tasks: Sequence[Task]
687	    ) -> None:
688	        """Reject a batch that names one robot id or task id more than once.
689	
690	        Each robot id may identify at most one robot within the given robot
691	        list, and each task id at most one task within the task list; the two
692	        namespaces are independent, so a robot and a task may share one string.
693	        The judgement is on the identifiers alone -- nothing else about two
694	        records can make a clash legal: identical records handed in twice are
695	        still duplicates, as are two robots differing only in position, idle
696	        state, preset route or in-flight task, and two tasks differing in
697	        pickup/dropoff points, owner or completion state (one finished and one
698	        still waiting included). A clash therefore never keeps one record,
699	        merges the two or renames anything: the whole request is rejected with
700	        a :class:`ValueError` that says whether the clash is among the robots
701	        or the tasks and quotes the duplicated id.
702	
703	        The check is read-only and runs before any normalization commits, so
704	        every caller object -- including records preceding a duplicate placed
705	        last -- keeps exactly the position, route containers, pickup/dropoff
706	        containers, bindings, mileage and flags it arrived with. Checkpoint
707	        loading keeps its own pre-existing duplicate rejection and wording in
708	        :meth:`_load_entities`.
709	        """
710	        seen_robot_ids: dict[str, int] = {}
711	        for index, robot in enumerate(robots):
712	            earlier = seen_robot_ids.get(robot.robot_id)
713	            if earlier is not None:
714	                raise ValueError(
715	                    f"duplicate robot id {robot.robot_id!r} in robot list: "
716	                    f"entries {earlier} and {index} both name the same robot; "
717	                    "each robot id may appear at most once in a construction "
718	                    "request"
719	                )
720	            seen_robot_ids[robot.robot_id] = index
721	        seen_task_ids: dict[str, int] = {}
722	        for index, task in enumerate(tasks):
723	            earlier = seen_task_ids.get(task.task_id)
724	            if earlier is not None:
725	                raise ValueError(
726	                    f"duplicate task id {task.task_id!r} in task list: "
727	                    f"entries {earlier} and {index} both name the same task; "
728	                    "each task id may appear at most once in a construction "
729	                    "request"
730	                )
731	            seen_task_ids[task.task_id] = index
732	
733	    @staticmethod
734	    def _normalize_start_positions(
735	        grid: GridMap, robots: Sequence[Robot]
736	    ) -> list[Position]:
737	        """Validate every robot's starting position and return tuple copies.
738	
739	        The position rule is deliberately the same strict rule the route
740	        waypoints use (:func:`_as_cell`): a position must be a list or tuple
741	        (the two spellings may be mixed across one batch) holding exactly two
742	        plain integers -- booleans are rejected even though they are Python
743	        ints, and floats, strings, missing components, extra components and
744	        non-pair inputs are all refused with :class:`ValueError` naming the
745	        robot and its bad position, never rounded, coerced or padded.
746	
747	        Every accepted position is additionally checked against the map: it
748	        must lie inside the grid and outside every obstacle. Two robots may
749	        not start on the same cell either; the comparison runs on normalized
750	        tuple values, so one robot spelling a cell as ``[x, y]`` and another
751	        as ``(x, y)`` is still a collision, and the error names both robots
752	        involved. Idle robots, task-bound robots and robots carrying preset
753	        routes are all checked -- no robot is skipped to make a batch pass.
754	
755	        The check is read-only: it returns a fresh tuple per robot and commits
756	        nothing itself. The caller assigns the tuples to the robots only once
757	        the whole batch (routes and task bindings included) has passed, so a
758	        later rejection leaves the caller's positions untouched, and the tuple
759	        copy means mutating an originally passed-in list after construction
760	        can never change the created fleet.
761	        """
762	        normalized: list[Position] = []
763	        occupied: dict[Position, str] = {}
764	        for robot in robots:
765	            position = _as_cell(
766	                robot.position, f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} starting position"
767	            )
768	            if not grid.traversable(position):
769	                raise ValueError(
770	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} starting position {list(position)} "
771	                    "is outside the map or inside an obstacle"
772	                )
773	            other_id = occupied.get(position)
774	            if other_id is not None:
775	                raise ValueError(
776	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} starting position {list(position)} "
777	                    f"is already occupied by robot {other_id!r}: robots cannot "
778	                    "share an initial cell"
779	                )
780	            occupied[position] = robot.robot_id
781	            normalized.append(position)

784	    @staticmethod
785	    def _normalize_task_coordinates(
786	        tasks: Sequence[Task],
787	    ) -> list[tuple[Position, Position]]:
788	        """Validate every task's pickup and dropoff and return tuple copies.
789	
790	        Task points share the strict position rule (:func:`_as_cell`): each one
791	        must be a list or tuple (the two spellings may be mixed within one
792	        task and across one batch) holding exactly two plain integers --
793	        booleans are rejected even though they are Python ints, and floats
794	        (even ``1.0``), strings, nulls, missing components, extra components
795	        and non-pair inputs are all refused with :class:`ValueError` naming the
796	        task and whether its pickup or its dropoff is at fault, never rounded,
797	        padded or coerced. This runs for every task regardless of state --
798	        waiting for assignment, en route to pickup, already carrying the goods
799	        or already completed -- so a malformed point in a finished historical
800	        record is refused at construction just like one in a pending task.
801	
802	        Coordinate validity is deliberately kept separate from reachability:
803	        whether a robot can currently reach the points is never judged here, so
804	        a well-formed task whose pickup is currently unreachable keeps waiting
805	        exactly as before, and a loaded task whose pickup cell has since been
806	        closed keeps the goods and its binding -- neither is an error.
807	
808	        The check is read-only: it returns a fresh integer tuple per point and
809	        commits nothing itself. The caller assigns the tuples to the tasks only
810	        once the whole batch (positions, ownership and routes included) has
811	        passed, so a later rejection leaves the caller's tasks holding their
812	        original pickup/dropoff containers, and the tuple copy means mutating
813	        an originally passed-in list after construction can never change the
814	        created fleet. A list and a tuple naming one cell normalize to equal
815	        tuples, so they can never make a robot miss a pickup or fail a delivery
816	        merely because of the container type.
817	        """
818	        normalized: list[tuple[Position, Position]] = []
819	        for task in tasks:
820	            pickup = _as_cell(task.pickup, f"task {task.task_id!r} pickup")
821	            dropoff = _as_cell(task.dropoff, f"task {task.task_id!r} dropoff")
822	            normalized.append((pickup, dropoff))
823	        return normalized

825	    @staticmethod
826	    def _validate_task_ownership(robots: Sequence[Robot], tasks: Sequence[Task]) -> None:
827	        """Reject impossible initial bindings between robots and tasks.
828	
829	        The very same ownership requirements back direct construction and
830	        checkpoint loading, so they live in exactly one place. The mutual
831	        binding only governs work still in progress:
832	
833	        * A robot that declares a task must name a task that exists, is not
834	          completed yet, and is assigned back to that same robot.
835	        * An unfinished task that names an owner must name an existing robot
836	          whose current task it is; an unfinished task with the goods already
837	          collected additionally must have an owner.
838	        * A robot can therefore never be claimed by two unfinished tasks: the
839	          second task's owner points at a robot that executes another task.
840	        * A completed task must carry the picked-up mark *and* a historical
841	          owner (a non-null ``assigned_robot``); see below.
842	
843	        Completed tasks are history, not work in progress, but the history must
844	        still be coherent: a finished task must carry both the picked-up mark
845	        and the id of the robot that finished it -- ``None`` means "no record",
846	        never an anonymous completion, even when the pickup point and the
847	        dropoff coincide. Neither gap is repaired (the owner is not filled in,
848	        the pickup mark is not flipped, nothing is reassigned or dropped); the
849	        fleet is rejected as a whole with a :class:`ValueError` naming the task
850	        and the exact contradiction. The historical owner itself is bound by
851	        none of the in-progress rules: it need not be idle or name the task
852	        back, may already work a new task, may have finished several tasks, and
853	        may even be absent from the fleet, so historical records never occupy a
854	        robot or take part in new task assignment. Unassigned, not-yet-collected
855	        tasks simply wait -- even when no robot can reach them -- and are not an
856	        ownership error. Nothing here rewrites a binding or drops a task; an
857	        inconsistent input is rejected as a whole, leaving the caller's objects
858	        untouched.
859	        """
860	        robot_by_id = {robot.robot_id: robot for robot in robots}
861	        task_by_id = {task.task_id: task for task in tasks}
862	        for robot in robots:
863	            if robot.task_id is None:
864	                continue
865	            task = task_by_id.get(robot.task_id)
866	            if task is None:
867	                raise ValueError(
868	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} executes unknown task "
869	                    f"{robot.task_id!r}"
870	                )
871	            if task.completed:
872	                raise ValueError(
873	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} executes task {task.task_id!r} "
874	                    "that is already completed"
875	                )
876	            if task.assigned_robot != robot.robot_id:
877	                raise ValueError(
878	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} executes task {task.task_id!r} "
879	                    f"but the task is assigned to {task.assigned_robot!r}"
880	                )
881	        for task in tasks:
882	            if task.completed:
883	                # A finished task is a fixed historical record: the goods must
884	                # have been collected and a historical finishing robot must be
885	                # named. The very same requirement backs direct construction
886	                # and checkpoint recovery, so a document that could never be
887	                # loaded again can never be built in the first place. This is
888	                # judged purely from the record -- even a task whose pickup
889	                # point equals its dropoff is not presumed collected -- and the
890	                # recorded robot is history only: it is never looked up, so it
891	                # may be retired, idle or already busy with another task, and
892	                # several completed tasks may name the same robot without ever
893	                # counting as occupying it.
894	                if not task.picked_up:
895	                    if task.assigned_robot is None:
896	                        raise ValueError(
897	                            f"task {task.task_id!r} is marked completed but was "
898	                            "never picked up and has no historical assigned robot"
899	                        )
900	                    raise ValueError(
901	                        f"task {task.task_id!r} is marked completed but never "
902	                        "picked up, even though historical robot "
903	                        f"{task.assigned_robot!r} is recorded for it"
904	                    )
905	                if task.assigned_robot is None:
906	                    raise ValueError(
907	                        f"task {task.task_id!r} is marked completed and picked up "
908	                        "but has no historical assigned robot"
909	                    )
910	                continue
911	            if task.picked_up and task.assigned_robot is None:
912	                raise ValueError(
913	                    f"task {task.task_id!r} is picked up but has no assigned robot"
914	                )
915	            if task.assigned_robot is not None:
916	                owner = robot_by_id.get(task.assigned_robot)
917	                if owner is None:
918	                    raise ValueError(
919	                        f"task {task.task_id!r} is assigned to unknown robot "
920	                        f"{task.assigned_robot!r}"
921	                    )
922	                if owner.task_id != task.task_id:
923	                    raise ValueError(
924	                        f"task {task.task_id!r} claims robot {owner.robot_id!r} "
925	                        f"but the robot executes {owner.task_id!r}"
926	                    )
